back: It proves the inducer is creating enough suction, which shows the vent path is open. If the vent is blocked or the tube is split, the switch stays open and the sequence stops before ignition.

front: What does a flame sensor measure and what is a typical reading?
back: The flame carries a tiny rectified direct current, measured in microamps, between the sensor rod and the burner ground. A good reading is usually 2 to 6 microamps, and a dirty rod gives a weak signal.

front: What is the usual cause of burners that light and shut off after a few seconds?
back: A dirty flame sensor is the most common cause, followed by a poor ground or reversed polarity. Clean the rod lightly with a fine abrasive pad and recheck the microamp signal.

front: What does a tripped rollout switch mean?
back: It means flames or hot gases escaped the heat exchanger, often from a blocked heat exchanger, blocked vent or poor combustion air. Find and fix the cause. Never just reset it and leave.

front: What does a high limit switch that keeps tripping usually point to?
back: Low airflow across the heat exchanger, such as a dirty filter, closed registers, a failing blower or high static pressure. Measure static pressure and temperature rise before replacing any parts.

front: Why can a 90 percent or higher AFUE furnace use plastic vent pipe?
back: A second heat exchanger cools the exhaust below its dew point, so the gas leaves at low temperature and water vapor condenses. The cool exhaust allows PVC or CPVC, and a condensate drain is needed.

front: How do you find furnace airflow from output and temperature rise?
back: CFM equals output in BTU/hr divided by 1.08 times the temperature rise. For 64,000 BTU/hr output and a 45 degree F rise, CFM is 64,000 / 48.6, which is about 1,317.

front: How do you clock a gas meter to check furnace input?
back: With other gas appliances off, time one revolution of the one-cubic-foot dial. Cubic feet per hour equals 3,600 divided by the seconds, and multiplying by the heating value gives BTU/hr.

front: An 80,000 BTU/hr input, 80 percent AFUE furnace produces how much heat output?
back: Output equals input times AFUE: 80,000 x 0.80 = 64,000 BTU/hr. The remaining 16,000 BTU/hr leaves with the exhaust gases.

front: How much heat does a 10 kW electric heater make, and what current does it draw at 240 volts?
back: It makes 10 x 3,412 = 34,120 BTU/hr and draws 10,000 / 240 = 41.7 amps. With the 125 percent continuous-load rule, 52 amps calls for a 60 amp breaker.

front: How does the output of an electric resistance heater change with supply voltage?
back: Power varies with the square of voltage. A 10 kW heater at 240 volts produces only about 7.5 kW if supplied with 208 volts, because 10 x (208 / 240) squared is about 7.51.

front: Why do variable capacity systems control humidity better than single-speed ones?
back: They run for long periods at low speed, so the coil stays cold and wet and removes moisture steadily. Single-speed systems cycle off before much moisture is removed.

front: What is the capacity of a one-ton mini-split in BTU/hr?
back: One ton equals 12,000 BTU/hr. Common mini-split sizes are 9,000, 12,000, 18,000, 24,000 and 36,000 BTU/hr, so a 12,000 BTU/hr unit is a one-ton unit.

front: What are the main parts of a ductless mini-split?
back: An outdoor unit with compressor, coil and fan, one or more indoor heads, a small refrigerant line set, a power and communication cable, and a condensate drain. There is no duct work.

front: What does an inverter do in a mini-split?
back: It converts incoming AC to DC, smooths it, and rebuilds AC at an adjustable frequency using fast-switching transistors. Changing frequency changes compressor motor speed and therefore capacity.

front: How do you calculate the speed of a two-pole AC motor from frequency?
back: Speed in rpm equals 120 x frequency divided by the number of poles. At 60 hertz a two-pole motor turns 3,600 rpm, and at 30 hertz it turns 1,800 rpm.

front: What do the fan affinity laws say about power and speed?
back: Airflow changes in direct proportion to speed, but power changes with the cube of speed. At half speed, a fan moves half the air and uses only one eighth of the power.

front: A blower uses 600 watts at 1,200 CFM. What does it use at 800 CFM?
back: Power is 600 x (800 / 1,200) cubed, which is 600 x 0.296, or about 178 watts. Slowing a fan by one third cuts power by more than 70 percent.

front: What is an electronic expansion valve (EEV)?
back: A metering valve whose needle is moved in small steps by a stepper motor under the control of the circuit board. Sensor readings let the board hold a target superheat as load and speed change.

front: What is an NTC thermistor and what does a failed one read?
back: A temperature sensor whose resistance falls as temperature rises. A typical 10 kilohm part reads about 10,000 ohms at 77 degrees F. An open or shorted reading means the sensor has failed and may trigger an error code.

front: How tight should a flare connection be and what goes on the flare face?
back: Use the torque value in the installation manual, for example about 10 to 13 foot-pounds on a 1/4 inch line. Put a drop of refrigerant oil on the flare face and never use thread sealant.

front: How low should you evacuate a mini-split line set and indoor coil?
back: Pull a deep vacuum to 500 microns or lower and watch the micron gauge for a stable hold. Moisture can damage an inverter compressor and clog an electronic expansion valve.

front: A mini-split's factory charge covers 25 feet. The line is 50 feet at 0.2 ounce per foot. How much do you add?
back: Only the extra length needs charge: (50 - 25) x 0.2 = 5 ounces. The rate of 0.2 is an example, and the installation manual gives the real value for each model.

front: What is an ECM blower motor?
back: An electronically commutated motor is a brushless permanent magnet DC motor with a built-in control module. It is more efficient than a permanent split capacitor motor and does not use a run capacitor.

front: Why must you wait before touching an inverter board after power is off?
back: Its capacitors hold a dangerous charge for several minutes. Wait the labeled time, then measure the DC bus voltage with a meter and confirm it is below about 50 volts before reaching in.

front: Why should you not chase suction pressure when charging an inverter system?
back: Compressor speed and the electronic expansion valve change constantly, so fixed-system targets do not apply. Charge by weight with the line length adjustment and verify with the manufacturer's method.

front: What are the three temperature ranges of refrigeration applications?
back: High temperature has evaporators near 40 degrees F or above, medium temperature holds boxes at about 33 to 41 degrees F, and low temperature holds frozen food at about 0 to minus 10 degrees F.

front: What is the cold-holding limit for potentially hazardous food?
back: The US food code sets it at 41 degrees F or below. Frozen food is held at 0 degrees F or lower for quality and safety.

front: What are walk-in cooler panels made of and what R-value do they have?
back: They have a foam core, usually polyurethane, between metal skins, typically 4 inches thick for coolers. A good panel is around R-28 to R-32.

front: Why do walk-in freezers have a heated pressure relief port?
back: When the door closes, trapped warm air cools and shrinks, creating a vacuum that makes the door hard to open. The port lets air move, and its heater keeps frost from sealing it.

front: How do you calculate wall heat gain through insulated panels?
back: Q equals U x A x temperature difference, where U is 1 divided by the R-value and A is surface area in square feet. For 520 square feet of R-28 and a 54 degree F difference, Q is about 1,003 BTU/hr.

front: How much heat must be removed to cool 500 pounds of food from 70 to 38 degrees F at a specific heat of 0.8?
back: Sensible heat equals weight x specific heat x temperature change: 500 x 0.8 x 32 = 12,800 BTU. Freezing the food would add much more latent heat.

front: What is TD in a walk-in and how does it affect humidity?
back: TD is the box temperature minus the evaporator coil temperature. A small TD of about 8 to 10 degrees F keeps humidity high near 85 percent, and a large TD dries the air and can dehydrate product.

front: How do you find the sensible capacity of an evaporator from airflow?
back: Q equals 1.08 x CFM x air temperature drop across the coil. At 2,000 CFM and an 8 degree F drop, capacity is 17,280 BTU/hr.

front: What are the three main defrost methods?
back: Off-cycle defrost uses warm box air while the compressor is off, electric defrost uses heater rods in the coil, and hot gas defrost routes compressor discharge gas through the coil to melt frost from inside.

front: What are the current and resistance of a 1,000 watt, 240 volt defrost heater?
back: Current is 1,000 / 240 = 4.17 amps, and resistance is 240 squared / 1,000 = 57.6 ohms. A heater reading open, or very low resistance to ground, has failed.

front: What ends an electric defrost cycle?
back: A termination thermostat or sensor ends it when the coil reaches about 50 to 55 degrees F. A fail-safe timer, often 30 to 45 minutes, stops the cycle if the sensor fails.

front: Why is there a fan delay after defrost in a freezer?
back: It holds the evaporator fans off briefly so water left on the coil refreezes instead of being blown into the box and onto product.

front: What is the purpose of pump-down with a liquid line solenoid?
back: When the box thermostat is satisfied, the solenoid closes and the compressor pulls refrigerant out of the evaporator until a low pressure control stops it. The next start avoids flooding the compressor with liquid.

front: Why do air-cooled condensers need head pressure control at low ambient temperature?
back: Falling condensing pressure reduces the pressure difference across the expansion valve, starving the evaporator. Fan cycling, variable speed fans or a flooded condenser design hold the pressure up.

front: What is the most common cause of high head pressure in restaurants and stores?
back: A dirty condenser coil clogged with grease, lint, leaves or cottonwood fluff. Clean it before checking anything else, using a brush or low-pressure water, and never a blade that bends the fins.

front: How much heat must be removed to make 1 lb of ice from 70 degree F water?
back: Cooling from 70 to 32 degrees F removes 38 BTU, and freezing removes 144 BTU of latent heat of fusion. The total is 182 BTU per pound of ice.

front: What is the latent heat of fusion of water?
back: It is 144 BTU per pound, the heat removed to turn water at 32 degrees F into ice at 32 degrees F with no change in temperature.

front: What happens during the harvest cycle of a cube ice machine?
back: A hot gas valve sends discharge vapor through the evaporator. The warmth melts the thin ice layer touching the metal, so the cubes slide into the bin.

front: About how long should a normal harvest cycle last?
back: Typically 2 to 4 minutes. A harvest longer than about 5 minutes points to low charge, a leaking hot gas valve or a failed valve coil.

front: Why is a flake or nugget machine called continuous?
back: Ice is scraped off the evaporator wall by a turning auger as it forms, so the machine never stops to harvest like a batch cube machine.

front: What does the water curtain on a cube machine do?
back: It keeps water from splashing into the bin and acts as a safety switch. If it does not open as ice falls, the controller sees a harvest fault.

front: What is the difference between descaling and sanitizing an ice machine?
back: Descaling dissolves mineral scale using an approved acid cleaner. Sanitizing kills microorganisms using a food-contact sanitizer. They are separate steps and need a thorough rinse between.

front: Why must bleach never be mixed with an acid ice machine cleaner?
back: The mixture can release chlorine gas, which is a poisonous hazard. Use only the approved products, one at a time, and rinse the system well.

front: Why does a dirty condenser cut ice production?
back: It raises condensing temperature and head pressure, so the compressor works harder and moves less heat. Output falls and the compressor may overheat.

front: What are the two main temperature classes of display cases?
back: Medium temperature cases hold fresh food at about 33 to 41 degrees F. Low temperature cases hold frozen food with discharge air near minus 10 to 0 degrees F.

front: What is the largest heat load on an open display case?
back: Infiltration of warm, humid room air through the opening. It is usually well over half of the total load, so a damaged air curtain raises case temperature quickly.

front: Name three things that can disturb a case air curtain.
back: Blocked discharge or return grilles, product stacked above the load line, and a fan or ceiling diffuser blowing across the front of the case.

front: Why can off-cycle defrost not be used in a freezer?
back: It relies on box air above 32 degrees F to melt the frost. A freezer is always colder than that, so it needs electric or hot gas heat.

front: What ends a defrost cycle, and what is the fail-safe?
back: A coil temperature sensor reaching its set point, commonly 45 to 60 degrees F, ends defrost. A fail-safe timer ends it anyway if the sensor fails.

front: What does an anti-sweat heater do?
back: It keeps door frames and glass above the dew point of the store air so that fog and water do not form on the case door.

front: What is the formula for heat moved by a water loop?
back: Q in BTU per hour equals 500 times GPM times delta T in degrees F. The 500 comes from 8.34 pounds per gallon times 60 minutes.

front: How many GPM per ton does a 10 degree F chilled water delta T require?
back: 12,000 divided by (500 x 10) equals 2.4 GPM per ton. A smaller delta T needs more flow per ton and more pump energy.

front: How much heat does a water-cooled condenser reject per ton?
back: About 15,000 BTU/hr, which is 12,000 from the building plus roughly 3,000 from compressor work. At a 10 degree F range this is 3.0 GPM per ton.

front: Which chiller compressor type is common above about 150 tons?
back: The centrifugal compressor, which spins an impeller to raise vapor pressure. Capacity is controlled with inlet guide vanes or a variable speed drive.

front: How does an absorption chiller differ from a compressor chiller?
back: It uses heat from steam, hot water or gas, with an absorbent such as lithium bromide and water refrigerant under vacuum, instead of a mechanical compressor.

front: Why does a low pressure chiller need a purge unit?
back: The shell operates below atmospheric pressure, so leaks pull in air and moisture. The purge removes those non-condensables.

front: Which EPA certification covers low pressure chillers such as those using R-123?
back: Type III certification covers low-pressure appliances such as R-123 chillers, and Universal certification covers all equipment types, so either one qualifies a technician to service them.

front: How is evaporator approach calculated?
back: Leaving chilled water temperature minus the refrigerant saturation temperature in the evaporator. For example, 44 degrees F water and 38 degrees F refrigerant gives a 6 degree F approach.

front: How is condenser approach calculated, and what is normal?
back: Condensing temperature minus leaving condenser water temperature. A clean condenser usually runs about 2 to 5 degrees F, and a high value suggests fouled tubes or non-condensables.

front: How do you convert kW per ton to EER?
back: EER equals 12 divided by kW per ton. For 0.60 kW/ton the EER is 20, and COP is EER divided by 3.412.

front: What does IPLV describe?
back: A weighted efficiency at 100, 75, 50 and 25 percent load, because chillers seldom run at full load. It rewards good part load performance.

front: What limits how cold a cooling tower can make the water?
back: The outdoor wet bulb temperature, not the dry bulb. Tower approach is leaving water temperature minus wet bulb.

front: How much water does a cooling tower evaporate?
back: About 1 percent of the circulating flow for every 10 degrees F of range. A 300 GPM tower with a 10 degree F range evaporates about 3 GPM.

front: How is tower blowdown calculated?
back: Blowdown equals evaporation divided by (cycles of concentration minus 1). At 3 GPM evaporation and 4 cycles, blowdown is 1 GPM.

front: Why does a chiller need a flow switch?
back: It proves water is moving through the evaporator before the compressor starts, which prevents the water from freezing in the tubes and splitting them.

front: What is a load calculation?
back: A calculation of the BTU per hour a building gains in summer or loses in winter, used to size heating and cooling equipment to the real building.

front: What problems does an oversized air conditioner cause?
back: It short cycles, so the coil runs too briefly to remove much moisture. The house feels cool but humid, and starts wear the compressor and contactor.

front: What is the conduction heat transfer equation?
back: Q equals U times A times delta T, in BTU per hour. U is the U-factor, which equals 1 divided by the R-value.

front: What is the heat gain through 400 square feet of R-13 wall at a 20 degree F difference?
back: U equals 1/13 = 0.0769, so Q = 0.0769 x 400 x 20, which is about 615 BTU per hour.

front: What is the solar heat gain coefficient?
back: The fraction of the sun's heat that passes through a window. An SHGC of 0.25 lets 25 percent of the solar heat into the building.

front: How do you calculate solar gain through glass?
back: Multiply glass area by the SHGC by the solar intensity for that orientation and time of day, with intensity in BTU/hr per square foot.

front: Which window orientation usually loads a house the most in the afternoon?
back: West-facing glass, because the sun is low and strong when outdoor air is already at its hottest.

front: What is the formula for the sensible load of an airflow?
back: Q equals 1.08 times CFM times delta T. The 1.08 equals 0.075 lb/cu ft x 0.24 BTU/lb-degree F x 60 minutes.

front: What is the formula for the latent load of an airflow?
back: Q equals 0.68 times CFM times delta W, where delta W is the moisture difference in grains per pound of dry air.

front: How do you convert CFM of infiltration from air changes per hour?
back: Multiply the house volume by ACH to get cubic feet per hour, then divide by 60. A 20,000 cubic foot house at 0.5 ACH leaks 166.7 CFM.

front: How much heat does one watt of electrical load add to a space?
back: 3.412 BTU per hour. A 1,200 watt allowance for appliances adds about 4,094 BTU per hour.

front: What is the sensible heat ratio?
back: The sensible load divided by the total load. A house with 16,961 BTU/hr sensible and 22,294 BTU/hr total has an SHR of 0.76.

front: What do ACCA Manual J, Manual S and Manual D cover?
back: Manual J calculates the load, Manual S selects equipment to match it, and Manual D designs the duct system.

front: How is a furnace's heat output found?
back: Multiply input by AFUE. An 80,000 BTU/hr input furnace at 80 percent AFUE delivers 64,000 BTU/hr to the air.

front: Why is a rule of one ton per 500 square feet unreliable?
back: Two houses of equal area can differ greatly in insulation, windows, leakage and climate. Use the rule only as a rough check, never to choose a unit.

front: What are the four main tools for controlling indoor air quality?
back: Source control, ventilation, filtration and air cleaning, and humidity control. Source control is usually the cheapest and most effective.

front: What is the ASHRAE 62.2 whole-house ventilation formula?
back: Q in CFM equals 0.03 times floor area plus 7.5 times (bedrooms + 1). A 2,000 square foot, 3-bedroom house needs 90 CFM.

front: What is the ASHRAE 62.1 breathing zone formula?
back: Vbz equals Rp times people plus Ra times floor area. For an office, Rp is 5 CFM per person and Ra is 0.06 CFM per square foot.

front: What is a main risk of an exhaust-only ventilation system?
back: It makes the building slightly negative, which can pull air from a crawl space or garage and cause backdrafting of atmospheric combustion appliances.

front: Why is indoor carbon dioxide measured?
back: It is an indicator of ventilation, not the main hazard. Outdoor air per person is about 10,000 divided by the indoor ppm minus the outdoor ppm.

front: What outdoor air per person does 1,000 ppm indoor CO2 suggest?
back: With about 420 ppm outdoors, the difference is 580 ppm, so ventilation is roughly 10,000 / 580 = 17 CFM per person.

front: What does the MERV rating describe?
back: The minimum efficiency reporting value, from 1 to 20, which states how small a particle a filter captures. Higher numbers capture finer particles.

front: What is the efficiency of a HEPA filter?
back: At least 99.97 percent of particles at 0.3 microns. HEPA filters are used in cleanrooms and portable room cleaners.

front: Why can a high MERV filter harm an HVAC system?
back: It raises pressure drop and may cut airflow, which can freeze a coil in cooling or overheat a furnace. Check static pressure and consider a deeper filter.

front: What is dew point?
back: The temperature at which air becomes saturated and water starts to condense. Any surface colder than the dew point collects moisture.

front: What relative humidity range limits mold and dust mites?
back: The EPA suggests 30 to 50 percent. Mold can grow on damp surfaces above about 60 percent, and dust mites thrive above about 50 percent.

front: How does an ERV differ from an HRV?
back: An HRV transfers only sensible heat between air streams. An ERV also transfers moisture, which lowers the latent load of humid outdoor air.

front: How do you find the sensible savings of a heat recovery core?
back: Supply temperature equals outdoor minus effectiveness times the temperature difference. Then use 1.08 x CFM x the temperature improvement.

front: What carbon monoxide level triggers investigation near an appliance?
back: Readings above 9 ppm, which is the EPA 8-hour outdoor standard. Find the cause, such as a cracked heat exchanger or blocked flue, and correct it.

front: What is the EPA radon action level?
back: The EPA action level is 4 picocuries per liter. At or above that level, mitigation such as a sub-slab depressurization system with a vented fan is recommended for the building.

front: What is superheat?
back: Superheat is how many degrees F the refrigerant vapor is warmer than its saturation temperature at the same pressure. It proves the vapor reaching the compressor has no liquid mixed in.

front: What is the formula for superheat?
back: Superheat equals the suction line temperature minus the saturation temperature at suction pressure. For example, 60 degrees F line temperature minus 50 degrees F saturation gives 10 degrees F.

front: What is subcooling?
back: Subcooling is how many degrees F the liquid refrigerant is cooler than its saturation temperature at the high-side pressure. It shows that the liquid line is full of solid liquid, not bubbles.

front: What is the formula for subcooling?
back: Subcooling equals the saturation temperature at liquid line pressure minus the liquid line temperature. On R-410A, 365 psig is 110 degrees F, so a 100 degree F liquid line gives 10 degrees F.

front: Why must the technician read the PT chart column for the right refrigerant?
back: Each refrigerant has very different pressures at the same temperature. At 50 degrees F, R-410A is about 142 psig and R-22 about 84 psig, so a wrong column gives a wrong saturation temperature.

front: Which charging target is normally used for a fixed orifice system?
back: A fixed orifice system is checked by target superheat. The manufacturer's chart gives the number using indoor wet bulb and outdoor dry bulb temperatures, usually with a tolerance near plus or minus 3 degrees F.

front: Which charging target is normally used for a TXV system?
back: A TXV system is normally charged to a target subcooling, commonly about 8 to 12 degrees F, because the valve holds superheat nearly constant on its own.

front: What superheat does a TXV usually hold?
back: A TXV usually holds superheat somewhere between about 8 and 12 degrees F, by opening and closing in response to the temperature at its sensing bulb on the suction line.

front: What pattern of readings suggests a low charge?
back: A low charge shows low suction and head pressure, high superheat and low subcooling. Little liquid reaches the metering device, so the evaporator is starved and the condenser holds little liquid.

front: What pattern of readings suggests an overcharge?
back: An overcharge shows high suction and head pressure, low superheat, high subcooling and high compressor amps. Extra liquid backs up in the condenser and the coil is fed too freely.

front: What readings point to a weak compressor with leaking valves?
back: High suction pressure, low head pressure, and low superheat and subcooling. Discharge vapor leaks back to the low side, so the compressor cannot build a normal pressure difference.

front: What is the formula for sensible heat in BTU per hour from airflow?
back: Sensible BTU per hour equals 1.08 times CFM times delta T. For 1,200 CFM and a 19 degree F delta T, that is 1.08 x 1,200 x 19, or 24,624 BTU per hour.

front: What is the condenser temperature difference?
back: It is the condensing temperature, read from head pressure on the PT chart, minus the outdoor air temperature entering the condenser. On R-410A, 365 psig is 110 degrees F, so with 95 degree F air it is 15 degrees F.

front: Why should airflow be fixed before the charge is adjusted?
back: Low airflow from a dirty filter or blower changes pressures, superheat and delta T. Charging in that state leaves the system overcharged once airflow is restored, so correct airflow first.

front: Why is weigh-in charging used in very cold weather?
back: In very cold weather the condenser cannot hold normal pressure, which makes superheat and subcooling readings misleading. Weighing in the nameplate charge by mass does not depend on outdoor conditions.

front: What does the blue low-side gauge on a manifold read?
back: The blue low-side gauge is a compound gauge. It reads positive pressure in psig and also vacuum in inches of mercury, so it can show pressures below the atmosphere.

front: What is the difference between psig and psia?
back: Psig is pressure above the atmosphere, read from a gauge that reads zero when open to air. Psia is absolute pressure and adds about 14.7 psi, so 142 psig equals 156.7 psia.

front: How can you check a service thermometer for accuracy?
back: Place the probe in a stirred glass of crushed ice and water. It should read about 32 degrees F. A reading of 35 degrees F means a 3 degree error that must be corrected or the thermometer replaced.

front: Why is an infrared thermometer unreliable on bare copper pipe?
back: Shiny copper has low emissivity, so it reflects heat from its surroundings instead of radiating its own. Covering a small spot with flat paint or tape gives a more accurate infrared reading.

front: Why must a clamp meter surround only one conductor?
back: Current flows in opposite directions in the two conductors of a circuit, so their magnetic fields cancel inside the jaws. Clamping both shows almost zero, while one wire shows the true current.

front: Why use a true RMS meter on variable speed equipment?
back: Variable speed drives and electronically commutated motors create distorted waveforms. A true RMS meter calculates the correct effective value, while an average-reading meter can be off by 10 percent or more.

front: What is a manometer used for in HVACR service?
back: A manometer measures air pressure in inches of water column. It is used to find total external static pressure, which is typically near 0.5 inches w.c. on a residential blower system.

front: What is the formula for airflow from air speed and area?
back: CFM equals velocity in feet per minute times area in square feet. A grille of 3.33 square feet with an average speed of 300 fpm moves about 1,000 CFM.

front: What does a micron gauge measure?
back: A micron gauge measures deep vacuum as absolute pressure in microns. A compound gauge cannot show this range. Many procedures call for 500 microns or lower before the system is charged.

front: What does a vacuum decay test show?
back: After valving off the pump, watch the micron gauge. A rise that levels off near 1,000 to 2,000 microns suggests moisture. A steady climb means a leak. A small rise that holds shows a dry, tight system.

front: Why should oxygen or compressed air never be used to pressurize a system?
back: Oxygen can react violently with oil and ignite, and compressed air carries moisture into the system. Dry nitrogen is the gas used for pressure and leak testing.

front: How full may a refrigerant cylinder be filled?
back: A cylinder must never be filled above 80 percent of its capacity by weight. The empty space allows for thermal expansion of the liquid so the cylinder does not become dangerously full.

front: What does a negative superheat reading mean?
back: It means vapor appears colder than its saturation temperature, which cannot happen in vapor flow. The cause is usually a poor probe contact, a faulty thermometer or the wrong chart, so recheck.

front: What is the difference between accuracy and resolution?
back: Resolution is the smallest step a display shows, such as 0.1 degree. Accuracy is how close the reading is to the true value. A meter can show fine steps and still be wrong.

front: What readings together indicate a low charge on a TXV system?
back: Low suction pressure, superheat near 20 degrees F, subcooling near 6 degrees F, low head pressure and amps below the rated load amps all point toward a low charge and a leak to find.

front: What are the six steps of the troubleshooting method?
back: Listen to the complaint, look at obvious items, check the electrical supply, check airflow, take refrigerant readings, then repair the cause and test again to prove the repair worked.

front: What voltage range is acceptable for equipment rated 230 volts?
back: Rated voltage usually allows about plus or minus 10 percent, so roughly 207 to 253 volts. Low voltage forces a motor to draw more current to deliver the same power and overheats it.

front: What should the voltage across a closed contactor's contacts read?
back: It should be near zero, no more than a volt or two. A reading of several volts across a closed set of contacts shows pitting or burning that wastes voltage meant for the motor.

front: What is the acceptable range for a 45 uF capacitor rated at plus or minus 6 percent?
back: The range is 45 minus 2.7 to 45 plus 2.7, which is 42.3 to 47.7 uF. A reading of 36.8 uF is more than 18 percent low and the capacitor should be replaced.

front: What is the field formula for capacitance from amps and volts?
back: Capacitance in uF equals 2,652 times amps divided by volts. With 3.3 amps and 240 volts, that is 2,652 x 3.3 divided by 240, or about 36.5 uF.

front: What symptoms does a weak run capacitor cause?
back: A weak run capacitor makes a motor hum, start slowly, run hot, draw extra current or fail to start. The compressor may draw near locked rotor amps and then trip its overload.

front: What is the rule for single-phase compressor winding resistances?
back: Start to run equals common to start plus common to run. With 1.9 and 1.2 ohms for the first two, start to run should read 3.1 ohms.

front: Why wait before concluding a compressor winding is open?
back: Many compressors have an internal thermal overload that opens the circuit when hot. After an hour or more of cooling it may close again, showing that the windings were fine and the motor was overheated.

front: What does a megohmmeter test from a compressor terminal to the shell show?
back: It shows winding insulation quality. A good reading is in the megohm range, often over 100 megohms. A reading of a few thousand ohms means the insulation has failed and the winding is grounded.

front: What are locked rotor amps?
back: Locked rotor amps, or LRA, are the current drawn at the instant of starting or when the rotor will not turn. It is often five to six times the running load amps on the nameplate.

front: What readings suggest a dirty condenser coil?
back: High head pressure and a large condenser temperature difference, such as 125 degrees F condensing with 95 degrees F air for 30 degrees F, with correct superheat and subcooling and slightly high amps.

front: What are non-condensables and how do they affect pressure?
back: Non-condensables are gases such as air that do not condense in the condenser. They raise head pressure. The cure is to recover the charge, evacuate to 500 microns and recharge by weight.

front: What clue points to a plugged filter drier?
back: A temperature drop of more than about 2 to 3 degrees F across the drier. A drop of 12 degrees F with high superheat and a starved evaporator matches a restriction.

front: What is a simple test for worn compressor valves?
back: Close the suction service valve and watch the low-side gauge. A healthy compressor pulls a deep vacuum quickly, while one with leaking valves cannot pull below a modest pressure and rises when stopped.

front: What should be done before replacing a burned-out compressor?
back: Find and correct the cause, such as low voltage, a restriction or moisture, then replace the drier and clean the system. Otherwise the new compressor is likely to fail the same way.

front: What is preventive maintenance?
back: Preventive maintenance is scheduled service done before a failure happens, to keep equipment efficient, safe and reliable and to find small problems while they are cheap to fix.

front: What is a service agreement?
back: A service agreement is a contract for scheduled maintenance visits. It gives the contractor steady work in slow seasons and gives the owner regular checks and earlier warning of larger repairs.

front: What water test checks a condensate drain on a maintenance visit?
back: Pour a small amount of water into the drain pan and watch that it runs freely. Clear the trap or line if needed and test the float switch, since a plugged drain causes water damage.

front: What is a baseline in maintenance records?
back: A baseline is the set of normal readings for a particular system, such as superheat, subcooling, amps and delta T, recorded at installation or a good visit so later readings can be compared.

front: What does a rising condenser temperature difference with steady superheat and subcooling suggest?
back: It suggests a dirty condenser coil. For example, going from 15 to 25 degrees F with the charge indicators unchanged means the coil rejects heat less well and the charge is correct.

front: How do you estimate power draw from SEER?
back: Watts equals cooling BTU per hour divided by SEER. A 3-ton system at 36,000 BTU per hour and SEER 16 draws about 2,250 watts, or 2.25 kilowatts.

front: What does 2.25 kW for 1,000 hours cost at 15 cents per kWh?
back: Energy is 2.25 kW x 1,000 hours, or 2,250 kWh, and the cost is 2,250 x $0.15, which is $337.50 for the season.

front: How does a clogged filter reduce capacity?
back: If airflow falls from 1,200 to 900 CFM at a 19 degree F delta T, sensible capacity drops from 24,624 to 18,468 BTU per hour, a loss of one quarter.

front: What should a technician do after finding a cracked heat exchanger?
back: Tell the customer clearly, advise keeping the furnace off, and document it in writing. A cracked heat exchanger can leak combustion gases including carbon monoxide into the air stream.

front: Which items matter most on a commercial refrigeration visit?
back: Condenser coil cleaning, defrost cycle checks, door gaskets, evaporator and drain inspection, fan motors, refrigerant charge readings and electrical connections, usually on a quarterly schedule.

front: Why should customers get options and written prices?
back: Options such as a basic repair, a better repair and a replacement let the owner choose, and written prices stated before work begins avoid disputes and build trust.

front: What are the EPA Section 608 certification types?
back: Core covers general rules. Type I covers small appliances, Type II high-pressure systems, and Type III low-pressure systems. Passing all sections earns Universal certification.

front: What does NATE certification show?
back: North American Technician Excellence offers voluntary exams in areas such as air conditioning, heat pumps, gas heating and commercial refrigeration, showing an employer the technician meets a recognized standard.

front: Why is a drifting capacitor reading worth recording?
back: A reading that falls from 44 to 43.5 to 42.6 uF may be in tolerance each time yet is clearly wearing out. Replacing it at a scheduled visit costs less than an emergency call.

front: Why should a technician avoid promising an exact savings figure?
back: Savings depend on use, weather and system condition, so an exact promise may be wrong and damage trust. Describe what was repaired, what was measured, and that results vary.
